report.summary: Claim 8.9 is unfalsifiable: 'signed/traceable receipt' is undefined; claim 8.10 is weak because 'never auto-promote' is contradicted by real-world systems (e.g., AutoML) that auto-promote with safeguards; claim 8.1 is weak as freeze-then-iterate is standard (e.g., CRISP-DM).
risks: 8.9 | high | 'signed/traceable receipt' is undefined; no mechanism or standard is specified, making the claim unfalsifiable and unenforceable. | Check if the document defines 'signed/traceable receipt' elsewhere; if not, the claim cannot be verified.

8.10 | medium | 'never auto-promote' is contradicted by systems like AutoML (e.g., Google Vizier, 2017) that auto-promote with human oversight; the claim ignores established practice. | Show that a production system with auto-promotion and human veto exists; if so, the claim is not universally valid.

8.1 | low | 'freeze an ExperimentSpec' is standard practice (e.g., CRISP-DM, 1999) and not novel; the claim is weak as prior art. | Compare with CRISP-DM phases; the freeze-and-iterate pattern is well-known.

8.11 | low | 'promote only through sealed owner-controlled path' is vague; no definition of 'sealed' or 'owner-controlled' is given. | Check if the document defines these terms; if not, the claim is unclear.
todos: Define 'signed/traceable receipt' with a concrete standard or protocol (e.g., cryptographic signature, audit log).
Clarify 'never auto-promote' to allow conditional auto-promotion with human oversight, or justify the strict prohibition.
Define 'sealed owner-controlled path' with explicit access control mechanisms.
Acknowledge prior art for the freeze-and-iterate loop (e.g., CRISP-DM) to avoid reinvention.

claims.claim: Every campaign freezes an ExperimentSpec, budget, tasks, metrics, baselines, and seed policy.
claims.why: This is standard practice in experimental design (e.g., CRISP-DM, 1999; Google's AI Platform Pipelines). The claim is not novel and describes a common methodology.

claims.claim: Build the base Forest for an exact source revision.
claims.why: The term 'Forest' is undefined in this section; it may refer to a project-specific concept (e.g., a code forest). Without definition, the claim is unclear. Prior art: version control systems (e.g., Git) build trees for exact revisions.

claims.claim: Select formulation, parent, one operator axis, model, and evaluation fidelity.
claims.why: This is a standard set of choices in machine learning experimentation (e.g., hyperparameter optimization, model selection). No novelty is claimed. Prior art: AutoML systems (e.g., Auto-WEKA, 2013).

claims.claim: Compile a minimal Context Capsule from verified project evidence.
claims.why: The term 'Context Capsule' is undefined; it may refer to a data structure or artifact. Without definition, the claim is unclear. Prior art: context-aware systems (e.g., Context Toolkit, 1999).
Isolated, bounded trials are standard in sandboxed testing (e.g., Docker containers, 2013; gVisor, 2018). The claim is not novel.

claims.claim: Store the candidate source tree in content-addressed storage.
claims.why: Content-addressed storage is standard in version control (e.g., Git, 2005) and package managers (e.g., IPFS, 2015). The claim is not novel.

claims.claim: Build a candidate Forest and revision-aware delta.
claims.why: The term 'Forest' is undefined; 'revision-aware delta' suggests differential computation, which is standard (e.g., diff algorithms). The claim is unclear due to undefined terms.

claims.claim: Run the evaluation cascade from cheap validity checks to held-out tests.
claims.why: Evaluation cascades are standard in machine learning pipelines (e.g., sklearn's Pipeline, 2007; MLflow, 2018). The claim is not novel.

claims.claim: Emit a signed/traceable receipt and archive all outcomes.
claims.why: The terms 'signed/traceable receipt' are undefined; no standard (e.g., cryptographic signature, audit log) is specified. Without a definition, the claim cannot be verified. Prior art: signed receipts exist (e.g., blockchain timestamps), but the claim is too vague.

claims.claim: Nominate successful candidates; never auto-promote them.
claims.why: Auto-promotion is common in automated machine learning (e.g., Google Vizier, 2017; Auto-Keras, 2018) with human oversight. The claim prohibits auto-promotion outright, which contradicts established practice. It may be intended as a safety measure, but it is not universally applicable.

claims.claim: Promote only through the sealed owner-controlled path.
claims.why: The terms 'sealed' and 'owner-controlled path' are undefined; they imply access control but no mechanism is specified. The claim is unclear. Prior art: role-based access control (e.g., RBAC, 1992).

claims.claim: Campaigns factorize evolution: change one major axis at a time unless a pre-registered interaction experiment justifies more.
claims.why: Factorial design is standard in experimental design (e.g., Design of Experiments, Box et al., 1978). The claim is not novel.

claims.claim: Code, prompts, operators, evaluators, and orchestration do not silently co-evolve in one campaign.
claims.why: Controlling for confounding variables is standard in scientific experimentation (e.g., randomized controlled trials). The claim is not novel.
